summary: You identify several important ethical issues, connect them to engineering pressures, and clearly conclude that shipping defective servers is unethical. Your discussion, external examples, and engineering ethics guidance provide a useful foundation. To strengthen the report, develop a practical risk-based decision method, weigh alternatives to rejecting the contract, deepen and qualify your evidence, and improve reference consistency and presentation.
next_steps: In “DICUSSION: To Ship or Not to Ship,” distinguish defect types and assess likelihood, severity, exposure, and effective mitigation. Use those factors to explain which defects, if any, could be acceptable for shipment and what evidence would support that decision.

In “The Most Ethical Path” and “RECOMMENDATION,” compare delaying shipment, further testing, remediation, and staged deployment with refusing the contract. Explain the consequences for affected stakeholders and set clear conditions for any safe delivery.

Strengthen research and presentation: explain the limits of the healthcare IT examples and avoid implying they predict this scenario’s risk without evidence. Complete and standardise reference details, and proofread the report for fluent, concise language; consider visual elements that clarify your risk analysis.

criteria.C1: You identify safety, data loss, professional integrity, commercial pressure, and reputation in the INTRODUCTION and discussion, and name stakeholders. This meets the Excellent level. Keep linking each issue to engineering design and organisational context, and make stakeholder interests explicit throughout.
criteria.C2: In “DICUSSION: To Ship or Not to Ship,” you acknowledge the competitive advantage of on-time shipping; “The Most Ethical Path” weighs that against potential harm. To reach Very good, examine both sides in greater depth and give clear decision-making guidance, rather than relying mainly on assertions or a blanket refusal.
criteria.C3: Your progression from competing arguments through “The Most Ethical Path” to the CONCLUSION is logical, and the conclusion follows from safety and integrity concerns. To reach Very good, build a more compelling chain of reasoning by assessing defect severity, likelihood, mitigation, and stakeholder consequences, then show how that analysis supports your conclusion.
criteria.C4: You use engineering ethics guidance and external examples, including NHS IT failures and Volkswagen, to support your discussion. To reach Very good, add more substantial, balanced evidence and connect it carefully to the server scenario. Clarify that the healthcare examples do not establish equivalent outcomes or quantify the likelihood of harm here.
criteria.C5: You include an abstract, introduction, discussion, conclusion, recommendation, and references. To reach Good, improve fluency through careful proofreading, add relevant visual elements to support your analysis, and provide a few fully verifiable, consistently formatted references; Reference [3] needs complete publication details.
